title: tshark
description: The command-line network protocol analyzer from the Wireshark project. Captures and decodes traffic on Linux (including Arch) with the same dissectors as the Wireshark GUI, plus capinfos, editcap, and mergecap for working with capture files.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`tshark` ships as part of the `wireshark-cli` package on Arch Linux (the GUI lives in the separate `wireshark-qt` package). Current stable Wireshark/tshark is the 4.6.x series (4.6.8 as of mid-2026), with 4.4.x as the previous long-term branch.

## 1. Install

```bash
sudo pacman -S wireshark-cli
```

This pulls in `tshark`, `capinfos`, `editcap`, `mergecap`, `dumpcap`, and `tcpdump`-style filter support via libpcap.

## 2. Allow capture without root

Live capture needs raw socket access. Add your user to the `wireshark` group instead of running as root:

```bash
sudo usermod -aG wireshark psdk
```

Log out and back in for the group change to take effect, then verify:

```bash
tshark -D
```

If this lists your interfaces without `sudo`, permissions are set up correctly. On Arch, `dumpcap` (the actual capturing binary tshark shells out to) has capabilities set via `setcap` by the package, so group membership alone is usually enough — no need to touch `/etc/sudoers`.

## 3. First capture

```bash
tshark -i wlan0 -c 10
```

Captures 10 packets on `wlan0` and prints a one-line summary per packet. See [Basic Usage](/tshark/basic-usage/) for the core workflow.
Getting Started.Basic Usage:
## Core flags

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-i <iface>` | Interface to capture on (`-i any` on Linux captures all) |
| `-c <n>` | Stop after `n` packets |
| `-a duration:<sec>` | Stop after N seconds |
| `-w <file.pcapng>` | Write raw capture to a file instead of printing |
| `-r <file.pcapng>` | Read from a capture file instead of a live interface |
| `-f "<bpf>"` | Capture filter (BPF syntax, applied while capturing) |
| `-Y "<expr>"` | Display filter (Wireshark syntax, applied while reading/printing) |

**Capture filters (`-f`) vs display filters (`-Y`)**: a capture filter uses BPF syntax (the same language `tcpdump` uses) and discards non-matching packets before they're even written to disk. A display filter uses Wireshark's own filter language and is applied afterward for viewing — it's far more expressive (protocol fields, comparisons, logical composition) but can't reduce what actually gets captured.

## Save then filter

```bash
sudo tshark -i wlan0 -f "tcp port 443" -w capture.pcapng
tshark -r capture.pcapng -Y "tls.handshake.type == 1"
```

This captures only TCP/443 traffic to disk, then later filters the saved file down to just TLS ClientHello packets.

## Reading with detail

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -V
```

`-V` prints the full protocol tree per packet (like the GUI's packet detail pane), instead of the default one-line summary.

See [Field Extraction](/tshark/field-extraction/) for pulling out specific values instead of full packet dumps.
Getting Started.Display Filter Syntax:
Wireshark's display-filter language (`-Y`) is what makes tshark far more precise than raw tcpdump output — it understands protocol fields, not just bytes.

## Field comparisons

```bash
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "ip.addr == 10.0.0.5"
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "tcp.port == 443"
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "http.response.code >= 400"
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "frame.len > 1000"
```

Operators: `==`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`; `eq`/`ne`/`gt`/`lt`/`ge`/`le` work identically and are sometimes easier to read in a shell string that already uses `!`.

## Combining conditions

```bash
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "tcp.port == 443 && ip.src == 10.0.0.5"
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "http.request || http.response"
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "!(tcp.port == 22)"
```

`&&`/`and`, `||`/`or`, `!`/`not` — same logical composition as most languages, and (unlike BPF) parentheses group freely without needing escaping tricks for the shell beyond the outer quotes.

## Field presence and containment

```bash
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "http.host"
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "http contains \"login\""
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "dns.qry.name matches \"\\\\.example\\\\.com$\""
```

A bare field name (`http.host`) matches any packet where that field is present at all — a quick way to filter to "just HTTP traffic," for instance. `contains` does a substring match on a field's raw bytes; `matches` takes a full regular expression.

## Slicing values

```bash
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "eth.src[0:3] == aa:bb:cc"
```

`field[start:length]` slices a field's bytes — here, matching just the vendor OUI portion of a MAC address.

## Filter macros for saved shortcuts

```bash
tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y "${my_api_traffic}"
```

Wireshark filter macros (defined in `dfilter_macros`, shared with the GUI) let you name a complex filter once and reuse it — mostly relevant if you already maintain macros in Wireshark's GUI and want the same names available from tshark.

## Discovering field names

```bash
tshark -G fields | grep -i tls
tshark -r cap.pcapng -V | less
```

`-G fields` dumps every field name and type this build's dissectors know about (tens of thousands of lines — grep it); reading one packet with `-V` and scanning the protocol tree is often the fastest way to find the exact field name for something you can see but don't yet know the identifier for.

Guides.Live Monitoring Loop:
A common pattern: capture continuously, ring-buffer to disk, and tail matching packets live.

## Ring buffer capture

```bash
sudo tshark -i eth0 -b filesize:102400 -b files:5 -w /var/log/pcap/ring.pcapng
```

Rotates through 5 files of 100 MB each (`filesize` is in KB), overwriting the oldest once the ring is full — good for a bounded, always-on capture on a low-storage Arch box.

## Live filtered view

```bash
sudo tshark -i eth0 -Y "dns" -T fields -e dns.qry.name -l
```

`-l` flushes stdout after every packet (line-buffered), which matters when piping into `less -R` or another process — without it, output can sit in a buffer for a long time on a quiet interface.

## Pair with `journalctl`-style following

```bash
sudo tshark -i eth0 -Y "tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0" \
  -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e tcp.dstport
```

Streams every outbound SYN (new TCP connection attempt) as it happens — useful for spotting a misbehaving process making unexpected connections.
Guides.Statistics Reports:
`tshark -z` runs any of Wireshark's built-in statistics engines against a capture and prints a report instead of per-packet lines.

## Conversation summary

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z conv,ip
```

`-q` suppresses the normal per-packet output so only the report prints. Lists every IP pair that exchanged traffic, with byte and packet counts in each direction.

## Protocol hierarchy

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z io,phs
```

Breaks down the capture by protocol layer (Ethernet → IP → TCP → HTTP, etc.) with percentage of total bytes at each layer — the fastest way to answer "what's actually in this pcap".

## HTTP request tree

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z http_req,tree
```

`tshark -z help` prints the full list of available `-z` report types; there are dozens covering DNS, TLS handshakes, RTP streams, and more.
Guides.Examples:
Index of runnable examples in this section.

| Page | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| [Live Monitoring Loop](/tshark/live-monitoring-loop/) | Ring-buffer capture and live-filtered tailing |
| [Statistics Reports](/tshark/statistics-reports/) | `-z` conversation, protocol-hierarchy, and HTTP reports |

*Part of the [Field Extraction](/tshark/field-extraction/) page.* Minimal end-to-end script: capture HTTP traffic for 30 seconds, then print every requested URL.

Source: `example/http_urls.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

sudo tshark -i wlan0 -a duration:30 -f "tcp port 80" -w /tmp/http.pcapng
tshark -r /tmp/http.pcapng -Y "http.request" \
  -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri
```

Run it:

```bash
chmod +x example/http_urls.sh
./example/http_urls.sh
```
Guides.Decoding TLS With Session Keys:
Most interesting traffic today is TLS-encrypted; tshark can still show you the plaintext if you can supply the session keys — this is legitimate for traffic you control (your own browser, your own server, your own app) and is exactly how browser developers debug HTTPS.

## Capturing keys as your own browser/app runs

Set the standard `SSLKEYLOGFILE` environment variable before launching the browser or app whose traffic you want to inspect — most TLS stacks (Chrome, Firefox, and Dart's own `dart:io` `SecureSocket` via the underlying BoringSSL/OpenSSL) honor it:

```bash
export SSLKEYLOGFILE=$HOME/tls-keys.log
google-chrome-stable &
```

Every TLS session's per-connection secrets get appended to that file as the browser negotiates them.

## Pointing tshark at the keylog file

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng \
  -o "tls.keylog_file:$HOME/tls-keys.log" \
  -Y "http2 || tls.handshake.type == 1"
```

With the matching keylog file, tshark decrypts the session on the fly and dissects the plaintext HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 payload inside, exactly like the GUI's *Preferences → Protocols → TLS → (Pre)-Master-Secret log filename* does.

## Server-side private key (older TLS ≤ 1.2 only)

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -o "tls.keys_list:0.0.0.0,443,http,/path/server.key"
```

For TLS 1.2 and earlier (where the key exchange doesn't provide forward secrecy by default), a server's RSA private key alone can decrypt captured traffic to it. This does **not** work for TLS 1.3 or any modern TLS 1.2 cipher suite using (EC)DHE — those require the keylog-file approach above regardless of who owns the server, since the session key is never derivable from the static private key alone.
Guides.Following Streams And Exporting Objects:
## Following a TCP stream

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -q -z follow,tcp,ascii,0
```

Reassembles TCP stream index `0` (find the index from a normal `-Y "tcp.stream eq 0"` filter, or by opening the file in Wireshark once) and prints it as ASCII — the CLI equivalent of *Follow → TCP Stream* in the GUI. Use `follow,tcp,hex,N` for a hex dump instead when the payload is binary.

## Exporting transferred files

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng --export-objects http,./exported_http/
```

Pulls every file transferred over HTTP in the capture (images, downloads, scripts) out into a directory, named by their original filename where available. Also supports `dicom`, `smb`, `tftp`, and a few other object-carrying protocols — `tshark -h | grep export-objects` for the current list.

## Combining stream reassembly with a display filter

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -Y "tcp.stream eq 3" -T fields -e data.data
```

Rather than the `-z follow` report format, filtering to one `tcp.stream` value and printing raw payload bytes per-packet is often more scriptable when you want to reconstruct a stream programmatically (e.g. in a Dart script) instead of just eyeballing it.
Guides.Decode As And Protocol Overrides:
Sometimes tshark guesses the wrong protocol for a stream — a service running HTTP on a non-standard port, for instance — and its dissection comes out wrong or empty.

## Forcing a port to a specific dissector

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -d tcp.port==8080,http
```

`-d <selector>,<proto>` tells tshark "treat this traffic as `<proto>`" regardless of the usual port convention — the CLI equivalent of the GUI's right-click *Decode As...*. Repeatable for multiple overrides in one run.

## Disabling a noisy or slow dissector

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng --disable-protocol http2
```

Occasionally useful when a dissector for a protocol you don't care about is either misfiring on ambiguous traffic or measurably slowing down processing of a very large capture.

## Passing arbitrary preferences

```bash
tshark -r capture.pcapng -o "http.desegment_body:FALSE"
```

`-o "<preference>:<value>"` sets any of the same preferences the GUI exposes under *Edit → Preferences* — the TLS keylog setting from [Decoding TLS With Session Keys](/tshark/decoding-tls-with-session-keys/) uses this same mechanism.

CLI Reference.tshark:
## Synopsis

```
tshark [options] [filter]
```

## Capture control

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-D` | List available capture interfaces and exit |
| `-i <iface\|->` | Capture interface; `-` reads from stdin |
| `-f <bpf>` | Capture filter (BPF syntax, applied while capturing) |
| `-c <n>` | Stop after `n` packets |
| `-a <crit>` | Autostop criterion, e.g. `duration:60`, `filesize:1000` |
| `-b <crit>` | Ring buffer option, e.g. `files:5`, `filesize:102400` |
| `-p` | Don't put the interface into promiscuous mode |
| `-s <bytes>` | Snapshot length per packet |

## Reading and writing

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-r <file>` | Read packets from a capture file |
| `-w <file>` | Write raw packets to a capture file |
| `-F <fmt>` | Output capture file format (default pcapng) |
| `-R <expr>` | Read filter, applied during a two-pass read (heavier than `-Y`, needed for some filters that depend on later packets) |

## Filtering and dissection

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-Y <expr>` | Display filter (Wireshark filter syntax) |
| `-d <sel>,<proto>` | Force a specific dissector (Decode As) |
| `--disable-protocol NAME` | Turn off a dissector entirely |
| `-o <pref>:<value>` | Set any GUI-equivalent preference (repeatable) |
| `-K <keytab\|keyfile>` | Kerberos keytab or TLS key file for decryption |
| `-2` | Enable two-pass analysis (needed for some stats and `-R`) |

## Output format

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-T <fmt>` | Output format: `text`, `fields`, `json`, `ek`, `pdml`, `psml` |
| `-e <field>` | Field to print (with `-T fields`); repeatable |
| `-E <opt>=<val>` | Field-print option, e.g. `header=y`, `separator=,`, `quote=d` |
| `-V` | Print full protocol tree per packet |
| `-x` | Print hex/ASCII dump of packet data |
| `-P` | Print packet summaries even when also writing with `-w` |
| `-n` | Disable all name resolution (faster, numeric output) |
| `-N <flags>` | Enable specific name resolution types only (`m`=MAC, `n`=network, `t`=transport) |
| `-t <fmt>` | Timestamp display format (`ad`, `r`, `d`, `e`, `u`, ...) |
| `-l` | Flush output after each packet (line-buffered) |
| `--color` | Colorize output using Wireshark's coloring rules |

## Statistics and objects

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-q` | Quiet — suppress per-packet output (use with `-z`) |
| `-z <report>` | Run a statistics report; `-z help` lists all report types |
| `--export-objects <proto>,<dir>` | Extract transferred files for a protocol into a directory |

## Misc

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-G <table>` | Dump an internal table (`fields`, `protocols`, `decodes`, ...) and exit |
| `-Q` | Quit immediately after the last packet, skipping cleanup delays |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show usage and exit |
| `-v` | Print version and exit |

Full option list: `man tshark` or `tshark --help`.
CLI Reference.capinfos:
Prints summary information about one or more capture files — duration, packet count, average rate, file hashes.

```bash
capinfos capture.pcapng
```

## Useful flags

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-c` | Show packet count only |
| `-u` | Show capture duration only |
| `-a` / `-e` | Show start / end time |
| `-T` | Output as a tab-separated table (good for scripting) |
| `-M` | Print sizes in bytes instead of human-readable units |

```bash
capinfos -T -M *.pcapng > summary.tsv
```
CLI Reference.editcap:
Edits or transforms capture files — splitting, deduplicating, time-shifting, or converting between capture formats.

## Split by packet count

```bash
editcap -c 10000 big.pcapng split.pcapng
```

Produces `split-00000.pcapng`, `split-00001.pcapng`, etc., each with 10,000 packets.

## Time-window slice

```bash
editcap -A "2026-09-17 09:00:00" -B "2026-09-17 09:15:00" \
  big.pcapng window.pcapng
```

## Deduplicate

```bash
editcap -d in.pcapng out.pcapng
```

Drops packets that are exact duplicates of an immediately preceding packet.
CLI Reference.mergecap:
Merges multiple capture files into one, ordered by timestamp.

```bash
mergecap -w merged.pcapng part1.pcapng part2.pcapng part3.pcapng
```

## Flags

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-w <file>` | Output file (required) |
| `-a` | Concatenate in the order given instead of by timestamp |
| `-s <n>` | Truncate each packet to `n` bytes on the way in |
| `-F <fmt>` | Output file format (default: pcapng) |

Useful with the ring-buffer pattern in [Live Monitoring Loop](/tshark/live-monitoring-loop/) — merge the rotated files back into one for offline analysis.

Project.FAQ:
### `tshark: Lua: Error during loading` on startup

A third-party Lua dissector plugin in `~/.local/lib/wireshark/plugins/` is failing to load. Run with `-o "gui.lua_enable:FALSE"` (or delete/move the offending script) to confirm, then fix or remove the plugin.

### Permission denied opening interface, even after joining `wireshark` group

Check that `dumpcap` actually has the capture capability set:

```bash
getcap $(command -v dumpcap)
```

It should show `cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin = eip`. If missing (e.g. after a manual reinstall), reinstall the package: `sudo pacman -S wireshark-cli`.

### `-Y` filter doesn't match anything I expect

Remember `-Y` is a display filter (Wireshark syntax), not a capture filter (BPF, used with `-f`). `-f "port 443"` is valid BPF; `-Y "port 443"` is not valid Wireshark filter syntax — use `-Y "tcp.port == 443"` instead.

### TLS traffic shows as encrypted even with a keylog file

Confirm the keylog file actually has entries for the session in the capture (timing matters — the log only gets useful lines once a handshake actually completes) and that the capture includes the *full* handshake from the very first ClientHello; a mid-session capture usually can't be decrypted even with correct keys, since key derivation depends on the handshake messages.

### `-z conv,ip` (or other two-pass stats) prints nothing

Some `-z` reports need `-2` (two-pass analysis) to see the whole file's context before reporting — without it, tshark may process too little to populate certain aggregate stats. Add `-2` alongside `-q -z ...`.

### JSON output (`-T json`) is enormous for a small capture

`-T json` includes the *entire* dissection tree for every packet by default, which is verbose. Narrow it two ways: filter first with `-Y` so fewer packets are emitted, or switch to `-T fields -e ...` naming only the specific fields you actually need, which is both smaller and easier to consume in a script.

Learn by Examples.Debugging A Dart App's Failing API Calls:
A Dart HTTP client is timing out talking to an API over HTTPS, and app-level logs aren't enough to tell whether the problem is DNS, TCP, TLS, or the API itself. This walkthrough uses tshark to see the whole picture, including decrypted request/response bodies.

## 1. Confirm the interface and permissions

```bash
tshark -D
```

Confirms the `wireshark` group membership from [Getting Started](/tshark/getting-started/) is working — interfaces list without needing `sudo`.

## 2. Enable TLS key logging for the Dart process

```bash
export SSLKEYLOGFILE=$HOME/dart-tls.log
dart run bin/my_client.dart
```

Dart's `dart:io` `HttpClient`/`SecureSocket` sits on the platform's TLS stack, which honors `SSLKEYLOGFILE` the same way browsers do — no code changes needed, just the environment variable set before the process starts.

## 3. Capture while reproducing the issue

```bash
sudo tshark -i wlan0 -f "tcp port 443 and host api.example.com" \
  -w /tmp/api-debug.pcapng -a duration:60
```

`-f` (capture filter, BPF syntax) narrows what's written to disk to just this API host on port 443; `-a duration:60` auto-stops after a minute so it doesn't need to be babysat.

## 4. Get the big picture first

```bash
tshark -r /tmp/api-debug.pcapng -q -z io,phs
```

Protocol hierarchy stats answer "did any traffic even happen, and at what layer does it stop" — e.g. if everything stops at the TCP layer with no TLS records at all, the problem is a network/firewall issue, not the API itself.

## 5. Check whether the handshake even completed

```bash
tshark -r /tmp/api-debug.pcapng -Y "tls.handshake.type == 1 || tls.handshake.type == 2 || tls.alert_message"
```

Looking for a ClientHello (type 1), a ServerHello (type 2), and any `tls.alert_message` — an alert here (e.g. a certificate error) explains a hang or failure before any HTTP request is ever sent.

## 6. Decode the session with the keylog file

```bash
tshark -r /tmp/api-debug.pcapng \
  -o "tls.keylog_file:$HOME/dart-tls.log" \
  -Y "http2" -T fields -e http2.header.name -e http2.header.value
```

With the matching keylog file, tshark decrypts the session and dissects HTTP/2 headers directly — showing the exact request path, headers, and status code the Dart client actually sent and received, in plaintext, without touching app code.

## 7. Follow the full decrypted stream for one request

```bash
tshark -r /tmp/api-debug.pcapng -q \
  -o "tls.keylog_file:$HOME/dart-tls.log" \
  -z follow,http2,ascii,0
```

Reassembles the whole HTTP/2 stream (index `0`) as readable text — the full request and response bodies in one block, useful for spotting a malformed request body or an unexpected error payload the Dart-side error message didn't surface.

## 8. Export the response body directly

```bash
tshark -r /tmp/api-debug.pcapng \
  -o "tls.keylog_file:$HOME/dart-tls.log" \
  --export-objects http,./api_responses/
```

If the API returned a JSON error body, this pulls it out as a file you can `cat` or feed straight into `jq` for inspection.

## 9. Turn a specific finding into a scriptable field extraction

Once the actual issue is identified (say, a slow-to-arrive final response packet), pull just the timing:

```bash
tshark -r /tmp/api-debug.pcapng -Y "http2.type == 1" \
  -T fields -e frame.time_relative -e http2.streamid -E header=y -E separator=,
```

CSV output like this drops straight into a Dart script via `Process.run` and `csv`/manual parsing, or into a spreadsheet, for a timing chart across repeated runs.

## What this walkthrough covered

`-D`, `-f` vs `-Y`, `-w`/`-r`, `-a duration`, `-z io,phs`, TLS alert inspection, `SSLKEYLOGFILE`-based decryption with `-o tls.keylog_file`, `-z follow`, `--export-objects`, and `-T fields` CSV output — the standard path from "something's wrong with this HTTPS traffic" to a decrypted, scriptable answer.
